about.text: Complainant HydraFacial LLC (formerly Edge Systems LLC), based in Long Beach, California, designs, develops, manufactures, and sells hydrodermabrasion systems, including its HydraFacial Syndeo, Elite, and Allegro systems. The named respondents are a group of companies that manufacture or distribute competing hydrodermabrasion products in the United States: Luvo Medical Technologies Inc. and Clarion Medical Technologies, Inc. (both of Ontario, Canada), Healthcare Markets, Inc. d/b/a Powered by MRP (Utah), Medical Purchasing Resource, LLC (Texas), Bio-Infusions USA Inc. (Florida), MIRAmedtech UG (Germany) and MIRAmedtech SP. Z.O.O. (Poland), and eMIRAmed USA, LLC (California).

Hydrodermabrasion systems are devices used for skin treatment that deliver liquid solutions, such as acids, antioxidants, and moisturizers, through a handpiece tip that contacts the patient's skin, using a vacuum to draw the fluid from a container to the skin and then away for disposal. HydraFacial asserts two patents covering such devices and methods for treating skin: U.S. Patent No. 11,446,477 (the '477 patent), which issued in 2022, and U.S. Patent No. 12,053,607 (the '607 patent), which issued in 2024; both claim priority to 2005-2006 provisional applications and are owned by HydraFacial. The accused products are the Bela MD, Cleopatra, and MIRApeel hydrodermabrasion systems. The Commission's notice of institution states the investigation covers claims 1-5 and 7-20 of the '477 patent and addresses whether there is a violation of Section 337 (the trade statute barring unfair importation practices) based on importation, sale for importation, or sale after importation of the accused products; the '607 patent was later withdrawn from the investigation according to one respondent's answer.

allegations.text: HydraFacial alleges that respondents violate Section 337 by importing into the United States, selling for importation, and/or selling after importation the Bela MD, Cleopatra, and MIRApeel systems. It alleges the Cleopatra and MIRApeel systems are manufactured in Germany and/or Poland by the MIRAmedtech entities and then imported and sold in the United States by respondents including Bio-Infusions, Medical Purchasing Resource, and eMIRAmed.

HydraFacial alleges that the accused products directly infringe, literally or under the doctrine of equivalents, the asserted claims of the '477 and '607 patents (a patent claim defines the boundaries of the invention that others may not use without permission). It also alleges induced infringement, contending respondents encouraged and instructed customers to use the products in an infringing manner, with knowledge of the patents from pre-filing cease-and-desist letters, and that the products are non-staple components especially made for infringing use.

To satisfy the domestic industry requirement (the complainant's U.S.-based activity tied to the patented technology that Section 337 requires), HydraFacial alleges it performs all research, development, and manufacturing in the United States at facilities in Long Beach, California, has invested millions of dollars annually in domestic research and development, employs a substantial domestic workforce devoted to the technology, and holds numerous patents. It alleges that its own HydraFacial Syndeo, Elite, and Allegro systems practice at least one claim of each asserted patent.

HydraFacial asks the Commission to issue a limited exclusion order (an order barring importation of infringing products from named respondents) under Section 337(d) barring entry of the Bela MD, Cleopatra, and MIRApeel systems and infringing components, and requests that a bond be imposed during the 60-day Presidential review period that follows any exclusion order.

answers.text: Respondents Luvo, Clarion, and Healthcare Markets deny violating Section 337 and deny that the asserted claims of the '477 patent are valid and enforceable, noting that the '607 patent has since been withdrawn from the investigation. Luvo admits selling the Bela MD for importation but denies importing it itself or selling it after importation, and denies infringement, arguing the Bela MD does not meet claim limitations such as the 'manifold system' and related fluid-communication requirements, and that indirect infringement is not shown absent direct infringement.
